nl_st_john_s_area.blurb: Climbing around the provincial capital, on the Avalon Peninsula, mixes roadside cragging and bouldering with wild sea cliffs. Bouldering is the bulk of it, centered on Blackhead, where small cliffs and boulders stand right beside the ocean, and on Freshwater Bay. Roped climbing is scattered: DFO (The Skerries) offers mostly trad and sport, Quidi Vidi has sport and top-rope lines at the Breakwater. Boulder problems are mostly V0 to V4 with a few reaching V8, routes are mostly 5.9 and 5.10, and a small number of ice lines, from WI2 to WI4, add a winter option.

nl_west_coast.blurb: The west side of the island of Newfoundland, spread across several hubs: Corner Brook, the Humber Valley, Stephenville and Gros Morne National Park. Sport and bouldering are the most numerous, with trad, ice and a lone mixed route filling out the rest. Rock climbs run from 5.6 up to 5.14, mostly 5.8 to 5.11, and boulder problems go from easy to V8. Gros Morne, in the Long Range Mountains, is known for winter ice and mixed lines, from several hundred to over 2,000 feet, graded WI4 to WI7 and beyond, with trips usually in January to March. Near Corner Brook, the Pasadena boulders sit inland in the forest, which makes them one of the milder spots on the island.

pa_safe_harbor_south.blurb: The southern half of Safe Harbor, a string of crags beside the Susquehanna River in south-central Pennsylvania, about 25 minutes southwest of Lancaster and a little below the dam. Nearly everything is bolted single-pitch sport, laid out along an old rail corridor, with a modest number of trad lines and a few top ropes. Grades run from 5.4 to 5.13, but the heart of it is 5.9 to 5.11, with moderates to spare. The rock is mostly a bit shy of vertical, with some steeper lines, and the style is fingery face climbing on slippery stone. Safe Harbor's crags face southwest and catch plenty of sun, so cool weather suits them best. Sectors include Electric Co., Autumn Arch, Hydroman and Numero Uno.

wa_minnehaha.blurb: A granite crag in John H. Shields Park, beside the Spokane River in the Spokane area, at about 1,900 feet. It holds a bit of everything: trad and bouldering lead, sport follows, with a single top rope. Grades run from 5.5 to 5.13, mostly in the 5.7 to 5.11 range, and boulder problems go from V0 to V6, mostly easy. The large river-facing Main Wall has the most routes, followed by Jurassic Park, with smaller faces such as Don Quixote Face and Secondary Face and many little rocks scattered for bouldering. It has both sunny and shady sections and can be busy or empty depending on the day and hour. The park also draws hikers.

ca_wonderland_valley.blurb: A large, open area in the Wonderland of Rocks section of Joshua Tree National Park, at about 4,200 feet. It is mainly trad, with plenty of multi-pitch, plus a modest number of sport and top-rope lines and just a couple of boulders. Grades run from 5.4 to 5.13, with the bulk between 5.9 and 5.11. The terrain is domes, towers and boulders, and the walk in takes roughly half an hour to an hour. The area is split into West and East. The west side has a high concentration of classic routes and is much more crowded than the east.

_skipped.ma_north_side: Only substantive pages (Dyke's Pond and Cape Ann on Mountain Project) are about its parent and grandparent; no page treats North Side as its own place beyond a sub-area list.
